slot.brief: Using the Rydberg relation, ask for the ratio or value of wavelength/energy for a transition in Lyman or Balmer, e.g. compare the n=2→1 and n=3→2 lines via 1/λ scaling; harder reasoning, so make the algebra slightly involved.

stem: In a hydrogen atom, an electron cascades from $n=5$ through $n=3$ to $n=2$. If the wavelength of the $4\to2$ line is $\lambda$, what is the total energy of the two emitted photons?

verdicts.working: The cascade photons’ total energy is the level difference for 5→2: \(Rhc(1/4-1/25)\). The given line has \(hc/\lambda=Rhc(1/4-1/16)\). The ratio is \(28/25\).

working:
$E_{5\to3}+E_{3\to2}=hcR_{\mathrm{H}}\left[\left(\dfrac{1}{9}-\dfrac{1}{25}\right)+\left(\dfrac{1}{4}-\dfrac{1}{9}\right)\right]=hcR_{\mathrm{H}}\dfrac{21}{100}$
$E_{4\to2}=hcR_{\mathrm{H}}\left(\dfrac{1}{4}-\dfrac{1}{16}\right)=hcR_{\mathrm{H}}\dfrac{3}{16}=\dfrac{hc}{\lambda}$
$\dfrac{E_{5\to3}+E_{3\to2}}{E_{4\to2}}=\dfrac{21}{100}\times\dfrac{16}{3}=\dfrac{28}{25}$

Independent check: The cascade photons’ total energy is the level difference for 5→2: \(Rhc(1/4-1/25)\). The given line has \(hc/\lambda=Rhc(1/4-1/16)\). The ratio is \(28/25\).
solution:
The total energy emitted in the cascade equals the energy difference for the transition $5\to2$.
$$E=hcR_H\left(\frac14-\frac1{25}\right),\qquad \frac{hc}{\lambda}=hcR_H\left(\frac14-\frac1{16}\right)$$
Thus, $\dfrac{E}{hc/\lambda}=\dfrac{21/100}{3/16}=\dfrac{28}{25}$, so $E=\dfrac{28}{25}\dfrac{hc}{\lambda}$.

draft.distractor_notes:
A: Counts only the photon from $5\to3$.
B: Counts only the photon from $3\to2$.
D: Uses $n=1$ instead of $n=2$ as the cascade endpoint.
